comments.author: rainbowzootsuit
comments.text:
Interesting. The Sequence of Operations we write for the data halls I work on specifically do not shut down the CRACs on smoke alarm for this reason. The International Mechanical Code (IMC) specifically allows this where a air handler over 2000 cfm serves only one space because it's recognized that it will not spread smoke around a building. 2000 cfm is the threshold where you typically have to install smoke detectors, and typically they do shut down on smoke detection.
The CRAC won't feed a fire oxygen as it's just recirculating the same oxygen depleted air.

comments.author: djoldman
comments.text:
Productivity and inflation are big subjects.
Just to touch on one important problem for which one must account:
Productivity over time is how much stuff you get out vs what you put in, from one time period to the next. Inflation is what the stuff costs over time.
But what do you do with stuff you used to make that you don't make now?
And the opposite: what do you do with stuff you make now that you didn't used to make?
If you look only at the the things that are almost exactly the same from one period to another, usually you find that the intuitions hold: food used to take 10% of our hours, now it takes .6%, etc. etc.
If you dig into the details of CPI and PPI, you'll quickly say, "waiiiiiit a second, can you really just do that?"
For example: they'll say that your tv or car now is "more stuff" because of "features." But if you had to make the old car now, you might be able to make way more of them for the same inputs.

comments.author: armcat
comments.text:
Just yesterday I saw a talk from Spotify where they presented their own fast retrieval mechanism "Parallel Fusion Router" [1]. It's also in the "learned retrieval" paradigm - in their case they use a teacher LLM to train a much smaller router LLM how to retrieve, using an LLM-as-a-judge based reward function.
From my own experience, these learned methods from Apple, Spotify and others, are highly relevant to hyperscale only - when you are dealing with hundreds of millions of items to choose from (or more), and require super high relevance in the top-5. For all other use cases (up to a few million items) I found that just building a BM25 index, and giving the LLM a BM25 "search tool" and casting a "wide net" wins every single time compared to learned methods (though the latter are more publishable in recsys and icml).
[1]
https://research.atspotify.com/2025/9/you-say-search-i-say-r...

Most embedding/BERT models are far too small to truly grasp the nettles when an AI ask questions to them; and if you condition the AI to only search for really basic things, then... you're basically back to grep + regex.
You need to prune all manner of useless detritus that might gum up your matches like test files, documentation, and sidecars that semantically overlap or you're just going to match your tests. That's fine if you're building a document store for a business, but if you want a "one-and-done" solution for your codebase it's rarely good enough.

That increased complexity, while less costly than before, still added time/cost to the project in terms of cognitive load and testing that otherwise wouldn't have been there had the design been "dumber".  This notion of increased design complexity could be thought of as a form of Parkinson's Law where the complexity of the design grows to fill the time available.
I think AI is certainly making us write code faster but how much time is really being freed up now that writing code is cheaper?  I get the impression that we are often just finding other things to fill that freed up time with, increased design complexity being one of those things.
